lessons.title: Speculation and Risk Management in Commodity Trading

children.text: MCX normally trades non-agricultural commodities like gold, silver and crude oil until 11:30 PM or 11:55 PM IST, depending on the US daylight saving calendar, which sounds like generous coverage of the trading day. It is not generous enough to cover NYMEX and COMEX, the US markets that actually set the benchmark prices MCX contracts are linked to, which keep moving on fresh news for hours after MCX has gone quiet for the night. Every single trading day, not just during a pandemic-era shock, a speculator holding an overnight MCX position in a globally-linked commodity is exposed to a window of price risk they simply cannot see or react to. Chapter 3 was about hedgers managing risk they already carry. This lesson is about speculators managing risk they have deliberately chosen to take on.

body.text: Speculative risk management in commodities comes down to three habits: size every position to a known, small, pre-decided loss; understand exactly where a stop-loss can and cannot protect you; and recognise when several 'different' positions are actually one large bet on the same underlying driver.

children.text: The Overnight Gap: A Standing Risk in Globally-Linked Commodities

markDefs.definition: The risk that a commodity's price moves sharply between when a market you are trading closes and when it reopens, so the next available price is meaningfully different from, and disconnected from, the last one you saw.

children.text: Chapter 2 covered how MCX crude oil settled at minus ₹2,884 a barrel on 20 April 2020, after WTI collapsed in New York hours after MCX's COVID-shortened session had closed. That was an extreme event, but the underlying mechanism,

, never went away. MCX's normal hours still end well before NYMEX and COMEX are done trading each day, and both are closed all weekend while global news keeps happening. A geopolitical shock, a surprise OPEC+ announcement, or a US inventory report can all move prices well outside MCX hours, and the first available MCX price the next session may simply skip past several price levels you were counting on.

body.text: Gap risk is highest for overnight and weekend positions in globally-referenced commodities: bullion, energy and base metals. It is lower, though not zero, for purely domestic agricultural commodities where the relevant news mostly breaks during Indian hours.

children.text: Position Sizing: Risking a Known, Small Slice of Capital

Chapter 1's leverage math showed that margin lets you control a contract worth far more than what you put up. Responsible position sizing works backward from that fact: decide the rupee amount you are willing to lose on a single trade before you place it, then size the position so a stop-loss hit costs roughly that amount, not whatever the margin happens to allow.

body.latex: \text{Lots to trade} = \frac{\text{Capital} \times \text{Risk \%}}{\text{Stop-loss distance per unit} \times \text{Lot size}}
body.caption: Round down to the nearest whole lot, since trading one lot more risks more than your planned amount.

body.title: Size a crude oil trade
body.prompt: Anjali has ₹5,00,000 in trading capital and wants to risk no more than 1% (₹5,000) on a single MCX Crude Oil trade. Her stop-loss is ₹50 per barrel away from her entry, and 1 lot is 100 barrels. How many lots should she trade?
body.explanation: Risk per lot = ₹50 × 100 barrels = ₹5,000, which exactly matches her ₹5,000 risk budget. So she should trade 1 lot. Trading 2 lots would risk ₹10,000, double her planned amount, purely because the position was sized to the margin available rather than to a pre-decided loss limit.

body.title: Now with a tighter risk budget
body.prompt: Farhan has ₹10,00,000 in capital and wants to risk 1% (₹10,000) on a trade. His stop-loss on MCX Crude Oil is ₹40 per barrel away from entry (lot size 100 barrels). What is the maximum whole number of lots he should trade without exceeding his risk budget?
body.explanation: Risk per lot = ₹40 × 100 = ₹4,000. ₹10,000 ÷ ₹4,000 = 2.5. Since a fraction of a lot cannot be traded, and rounding up to 3 lots would risk ₹12,000, exceeding his budget, Farhan should round down to 2 lots, risking ₹8,000, comfortably within his limit.

children.text: Stop-Losses: What They Do, and Where They Fail

A stop-loss order instructs your broker to exit a position once price crosses a level you set, and it is a genuinely useful discipline tool for a market that trades continuously during the day. It does not protect you from a gap. If price jumps straight from above your stop level to well below it, without trading at any price in between, your stop can only execute at the first available price after the jump, not at your chosen level. The April 2020 MCX crude oil settlement is the extreme version of this: no stop-loss placed anywhere near a normal price would have saved a trader from a contract that settled at minus ₹2,884, because the move happened entirely outside MCX's trading window, in a single overnight jump reflected only at the next settlement.

body.text: A stop-loss protects you from a slow bleed during trading hours. It offers little to no protection from a genuine gap. That is precisely why position sizing, which limits the damage even if your stop fails to execute where you expected, matters more than the stop-loss order itself.

children.text: A trader who goes long gold, long silver and long crude oil at the same time may believe they hold three separate trades. In practice, all three often respond to the same handful of macro drivers, a weakening US dollar, falling US real interest rates, or a broad 'risk-on' shift in global sentiment, and can fall together just as easily as they can rise together.

body.caption: Shared drivers that can make 'different' commodity positions move together

cells: Gold, silver, crude oil, base metals (most are dollar-priced globally)
Crude oil, copper, other base metals
Silver and base metals tend to move with risk appetite more than gold, which often holds a safe-haven bid even in risk-off moves

body.text: If your position sizing budgets 1% of capital per 'trade,' but three of your trades are really one large dollar-driven bet, your actual risk on that single macro view could be three times what you intended.

body.title: Before you place a speculative commodity trade
steps: Decide the rupee amount you are willing to lose on this trade before entering, as a small, fixed percentage of your total trading capital.
Size your position from that risk amount and your stop-loss distance, not from how much margin your broker will let you deploy.
If you plan to hold overnight or over a weekend, in a globally-linked commodity, accept that a gap could move the price well beyond your stop before it can execute.
Check whether other open positions share a common driver (the dollar, global growth, risk sentiment) before treating them as independent bets.
Confirm your total position stays within your own risk budget and within the SEBI/exchange client-level position limits covered in Chapter 1.

body.title: Weekend risk
body.scenario: Rohit has an open long position in MCX Crude Oil going into a weekend, with a stop-loss set at ₹200 below his entry price. Over the weekend, unexpected news breaks that would normally move crude prices sharply lower.
body.prompt: Explain what protection Rohit's stop-loss actually offers here, and what he should have considered before holding the position over the weekend.
body.modelAnswer: Rohit's stop-loss offers no protection against the weekend news, since MCX is closed and cannot execute any order until trading resumes. If the news is severe enough, MCX crude oil could open Monday well below his ₹200 stop level, and his stop would trigger at that much worse opening price, not at his intended ₹200 loss. Before holding over the weekend, Rohit should have sized his position assuming the worst plausible weekend gap, not just his stated stop distance, or considered flattening or reducing the position ahead of the weekend if he was not prepared to absorb a larger-than-planned loss.

cards.definition: The risk that price moves sharply between a market's close and reopening, so the next available price skips past levels you were relying on, including your stop-loss.
Choosing the size of a trade based on a pre-decided maximum rupee loss and your stop-loss distance, rather than the maximum margin available.
An order that exits a position once price crosses a chosen level, effective during continuous trading but not protective against a price gap.
Holding several positions that appear independent but actually share a common underlying driver, making the true combined risk larger than intended.

points: MCX's trading hours, even at their longest, end before the US markets that set global benchmark prices are done trading, creating a standing gap-risk window for globally-linked commodities.
Size positions from a pre-decided, small percentage of capital you are willing to lose, using your stop-loss distance, not from the maximum margin your broker allows.
A stop-loss protects you during continuous trading but offers little protection against a genuine price gap, as the April 2020 MCX crude oil settlement showed in the most extreme way possible.
Positions in different commodities can share hidden common drivers, like the US dollar or global growth sentiment, turning several 'separate' trades into one larger, correlated bet.
A practical checklist, covering risk budget, position sizing, gap exposure, correlation, and regulatory position limits, should run before every speculative trade, not after a loss.
